doc.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, November 11, 2017 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Why he dislikes the word artistic; innovators being too different
summary: Gates says Parker, Coltrane and Monk were innovators rather than self-styled artists and were first rejected for being different.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Why don’t you like the word “artistic”?

It gets thrown around too easy. “Oh I’m an artist.” Really? You paint? That’s what I think. An artist is somebody who creates a sculpture or a painting or something. I mean there are some guys that are musical artists. Let me go back to I hear Charlie Parker was an artist. No he wasn’t. Maybe he was a genius I don’t know. Maybe he was an artist. Maybe he was. But to me he was an innovator. And I don’t think he set out to be one, it happens. I don’t think John Coltrane sat down in his living room one day and said — you know — I mean I think he was reaching but I don’t think he said, I think tonight I’m going to do this just to sound different. I think he was reaching and he didn’t know what he was reaching for, and if you keep reaching maybe you’ll get to touch it. I don’t know. I mean Monk played different. Maybe he set out to play different but I don’t think he had a formula for what he was going to do. “I think I’m going to end a lot of my songs with that five and flat five together, bling.” I think it just happened. But it happened because he was open to being different. Then again, if you’re too different, “Oh that’s too © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

different baby, we can’t use you, sorry.” I mean those guys weren’t even recognized at first because they were too different. “You’re too different man, can’t you just fall in?” “Well if I fall in then I’m going to be just like everybody else.”
Yeah. Like Lester was going to be like Coleman Hawkins, remember?
